newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa said close to decision on navy buys.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa said close to decision on navy buys.

text.p: Parliament's adoption later this month of a post-apartheid defence review is likely to commit South Africa to the purchase of ships and submarines for its rundown navy, a senior legislator said on Wednesday.

Tony Yengeni, a former African National Congress (ANC) guerrilla fighter who heads parliament's powerful joint standing committee on defence, said the defence review would be submitted to the cabinet on May 14 and to parliament on May 19.
He told a news conference the review would propose a honed-down permanent core defence force with a better balance between navy, air force and army than there was under white rule.
South Africa's apartheid government, ousted by President Nelson Mandela's ANC in 1994, built up a powerful army to fight land wars against black liberation armies in Angola and Namibia.

But Yengeni said the review, commissioned by the government as a framework for future policy-making, written by the defence ministry and revised by his committee, would change the balance between the arms of the defence force.
"The principle we are following is that it will be a relatively smaller, tighter regular force than we had in the past and a part-time force that will support that regular force," he said.

But he added that a consequence of the balance would be that the navy, which now comprises two full-sized supply ships, a trio of 30-year-old French conventional submarines and a flotilla of inshore patrol boats, would have to be re-equipped.
"We have effectively agreed on having both a surface and an underwater capability - that means ships, that means submarines. It stands to reason it must have this basic equipment," he said.
Yengeni pointed out that Mandela recently gave his personal backing to the defence review and the revival of a navy to guard the Cape sea route between the Indian and Atlantic oceans.
"I expect that the defence review will herald the renaissance of the South African navy, the maritime shield of the nation and the guardian of our seas," Mandela told a naval parade recently.

Defence analysts saw Mandela's comment as a green light to resume an acquisition programme he had halted more than a year previously because he said public opinion was against the purchase of new ships.
The navy has narrowed its hunt for four corvettes, like European light frigates, to 1.6 billion rand offers by Britain's Yarrow Shipbuilders and Spain's Bazan shipyard.
Defence ministry sources have told Reuters that countries including Germany, France and Russia are pressing for inclusion in a new round of tenders.

But a senior ministry source said Britain could have a lead because it had linked the corvette tender to an offer of four unused Upholder class submarines mothballed in a Scottish harbour for around two billion rand.
Despite inflation of around nine percent, South Africa's defence budget was cut in March from 10.2 billion rand in fiscal 1996/97 to 9.5 billion rand for the current financial year.
